paper_title: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Existing sequential recommenders usually allocate a fixed computational budget to every item in a user's interaction history, regardless of the item's contribution to the final prediction. We challenge this de facto design with two diagnostic findings. (1) Non-uniform computational need: items within the same sequence vary drastically in how much computation they require. Most converge after shallow processing while a critical minority only stabilizes at full depth. (2) Suboptimality of fixed allocation: given oracle access to the target item, a non-uniform depth assignment consistently outranks the fixed one, indicating that existing uniform computation both wastes capacity on already-converged items and sacrifices overall recommendation quality. These observations motivate a shift from fixed-depth computation to item-level adaptive reasoning. To this end, we propose LoopRec. LoopRec recursively applies a single weight-shared block and introduces a lightweight gate at each recursion boundary that makes a binary exit-or-continue decision for every item independently. Items whose representations have sufficiently matured exit early, while those requiring deeper reasoning continue to subsequent recursions. This design converts the fixed global depth into a learned, per-item property without auxiliary depth labels, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks with four backbone families demonstrate that LoopRec consistently outperforms matched fixed-depth counterparts. Further analysis reveals that LoopRec's learned allocation exhibits interpretable patterns aligned with our post-hoc oracle analysis: lower-frequency items and more recent interactions naturally receive deeper computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Elpmis117/LoopRec.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Sequential recommendation models temporal patterns in user in-
teraction histories to predict the next item of interest, support-
ing personalized ranking on e-commerce and online content plat-
forms [12, 26, 27]. The dominant paradigm processes a user’s inter-
action history through a fixed number of stacked layers, producing
item representations that are then scored against candidates for
next-item prediction. This paradigm has driven steady progress
over the years, from attention-based models [10, 12, 27] to architec-
tures incorporating frequency-domain inductive biases [3, 26, 36]
and linear recurrences [16, 32, 35]. Despite their architectural di-
versity, these methods share a common and largely unquestioned
design choice: every item in the history receives exactly the same
computational depth.
sections.content: We argue that this uniform allocation mismatches the nature of user behavior. real-world interaction history is inherently heterogeneous [20, 37]: it mixes routine repeat purchases that carry minimal predictive signal with rare, exploratory, or pivotal interactions that critically shape the users evolving intent. Intuitively, these items should not demand the same amount of reasoning, yet current models are structurally incapable of differentiating between them, leading to suboptimal performance. To move beyond intuition, we design two diagnostic experiments on trained three-layer SASRec model (Section 2). First, we find that 76.14% of items already stabilize their contribution to the recommendation after single layer, while 6.72% remain sensitive through all three layers, and these two extremes frequently coexist within the same sequence. Second, restricted oracle equipped with groundtruth target information finds the original fixed-depth allocation optimal in only 4.6% of sequences, achieving up to 8.8% relative Hit Rate improvement through flexible reassignment. These findings show that: uniform depth both wastes capacity on items that have already converged and under-serves the critical minority that benefits from deeper computation. This motivates us to reframe sequential recommendation as per-item computation allocation problem. Conference17, July 2017, Washington, DC, USA Zhanshuo Cao et al. Realizing per-item adaptive computation in sequential recommendation, however, introduces two intertwined challenges. (1) Representation alignment across depths: since different items may exit at different depths, their output representations still need to reside in shared feature space for downstream computation and scoring. Allowing depth to vary without careful architectural design can lead to misaligned representations that are incomparable at prediction time. (2) Progressive depth determination: how much computation each item needs cannot rely on single upfront decision, because an items readiness only becomes apparent as it progressively absorbs context from surrounding items. Premature commitment risks either wasting computation on alreadyconverged items or prematurely halting those that have not yet formed reliable representation. We propose LoopRec, framework for sequential recommendation with item-level adaptive recursion. For representation alignment, LoopRec uses recursive architecture [1, 2, 29, 41], reusing single weight-shared block across all depths. Since every recursion maps through the same parameters, items exiting at any depth naturally produce representations in the same feature space. For progressive depth determination, LoopRec places lightweight binary gate at each recursion boundary that evaluates each items current state after absorbing the latest round of context, and decides whether it is ready to exit or should proceed to the next recursion. Items exit progressively as they converge, while those that benefit from deeper reasoning remain active. This design requires no auxiliary depth labels, introduces minimal additional parameters, and is readily adaptable to diverse backbone architectures. We conduct extensive experiments on three public benchmarks with four different backbone families. LoopRec consistently outperforms the matched fixed-depth counterpart. Beyond accuracy gains, in-depth analysis of the learned routing reveals interpretable allocation patterns aligned with our post-hoc oracle analysis: the model naturally devotes deeper computation to lower-frequency items and more recent interactions, precisely the groups that an oracle would also allocate more computation to. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We use two complementary diagnostics to reveal variation in item-level computational demand and the limitations of fixeddepth processing in sequential recommendation. We propose LoopRec, which combines shared recursive backbone with learned item-level stopping decisions to adapt computation depth within each interaction history. Experiments on three datasets and four backbones show consistent ranking improvements, with routing analyses revealing deeper computation for less frequent and more recent items.

3.2 LoopRec Architecture
Section 2 shows that different historical items within the same
sequence can require different amounts of computation, making
uniform fixed-depth processing restrictive for sequential recommen-
dation. Motivated by this observation, LoopRec allocates computa-
tion depth at the item level while keeping the standard next-item
prediction objective unchanged. For each position 𝑡, let e𝑣𝑡 ∈ R𝑑
and p𝑡 ∈ R𝑑 denote the item and positional embeddings, and let
x𝑡 = 𝜙 (e𝑣𝑡 + p𝑡 ) be the corresponding input token. Stacking these
tokens gives the padded input sequence X = [x1, . . . , x𝑇 ] ∈ R𝑇 ×𝑑 .
To realize this adaptive-depth mechanism within a single model,
LoopRec treats the backbone block as a reusable computation unit

3.3 Training Objective
The key additional component in LoopRec, compared with a fixed-
depth sequential recommender, is the depth router. Training there-

First, it should allocate different positions to different depths. Oth-

remain trainable throughout optimization. Because routing deci-
sions are made recursively, gates that become too hard too early can
lock the model into unstable depth assignments before the hidden
states are well formed. The objective design below is organized
around these two requirements.

4 Experiments
4.1 Experimental Setup
Datasets. We evaluate LoopRec on three Amazon Reviews 2023
categories [9]: Software, Office Products (Office), and Patio, Lawn
& Garden (Patio). These categories provide varied sequence and
sparsity regimes under a shared data source and preprocessing
protocol. For each category, we sort interactions by time and retain
users with at least 10 interactions. We use a leave-one-out split for
validation and test sets. During evaluation, we trim each history
to warm-start items so that all conditioning items have appeared
in the training split. The maximum sequence length is set to 50.
Dataset statistics are summarized in Table 2.
Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate all models with full-ranking top-
𝐾 metrics [13]. MRR measures the rank of the first relevant item,
while NDCG accounts for the position-discounted ranking qual-
ity of the held-out next item [11]. We report MRR@10, MRR@20,
NDCG@10, and NDCG@20 in the main results. Model selection
and early stopping use validation NDCG@20.
Backbones. LoopRec is instantiated on four widely used backbone
families to test its compatibility with different sequence modeling

is not limited to a particular backbone family or dataset. The gains
are also aligned across MRR and NDCG within each backbone block,
indicating that the improvement is not an artifact of a single met-

computation with item-level adaptive depth leads to consistently

(2) Gains transfer across backbone architectures. For attention-
based models, LoopRec improves NDCG@20 by 2.19–5.68% on

gains on Office and Patio, reaching 13.18% and 37.02%, respectively.

these results support the applicability of item-level adaptive re-

In such data, different history items may carry uneven amounts of useful context, so applying the same computation depth to every position can be less suitable. LoopRec can instead stop processing simple positions at an earlier recursion boundary and spend deeper computation on positions that need more contextual modeling.

sections.title:
4.3 What Shapes LoopRec’s Learned Depth?
Having established that LoopRec improves ranking accuracy, we
next ask what its learned depth allocation captures. Our analysis
focuses on position- and item-level factors, and finally connects
LoopRec’s learned routing back to the saturation-depth probe of
Section 2. Unless otherwise specified, the analyses in this section
use SASRec as the backbone and Office as the dataset.
sections.content: The router uses multiple effective depths rather than single near-fixed path (Appendix A.4). We examine this variation from three views: the relative position of the item in the history, its training-time frequency, and the depth-sensitivity pattern that the same item shows under fixed-depth reference recommender.

4.3.1 Depth by Sequence Position. A natural starting point is the
relative position of an item in the history. For each test sequence,
we divide the valid history into ten deciles, from the earliest inter-
actions to the most recent ones, and compute the average selected
recursion round within each decile. To give a broader view than a
single setting, we report four SASRec-backbone cases covering Of-
fice and Patio under two LxRy configurations, where each recursion
round applies 𝑥 shared blocks and at most 𝑦 rounds are available.
Recent history items are routed deeper on average. Figure 4
shows an average tendency for later history deciles to receive larger
selected rounds in the four cases. This suggests that relative position
is associated with depth allocation: recent interactions tend to carry
stronger signals about the user’s current preference, so LoopRec
assigns more of its depth budget to the later part of the history. The

4.3.2 Depth by Item-Level Factors. Position alone does not fully
describe a history item. Two items at the same relative position
can differ in how often they appear during training and in how
much context is needed to interpret them. We therefore ask whether
routed depth also correlates with item-level signals. As a focused
diagnostic, we bucket test-set history tokens by the corresponding
item’s training-time interaction frequency and report the resulting
depth statistics in Table 4.
Frequent items are assigned shallower depths, while rarer
items receive more computation. As training frequency in-
creases, the mean selected depth generally decreases from 2.160
in the single-occurrence bucket to 1.330 in the 100+ bucket. The
share of depth-1 assignments rises from 50.3% to 88.6%, while the
share of depth-4 assignments drops from 29.1% to 10.7%. Routed
depth therefore correlates not only with position but also with
the sparsity of item-level interaction signals. This suggests that
frequent items form stable representations with little additional
computation, while rarer items more often benefit from later recur-
sive updates. Appendix A.5 complements these aggregate statistics
with a category-level view and a full sequence example illustrating
the routing patterns.
sections.content: The observed relationships between depth, recency, and frequency motivate testing whether simple routing rules based on these signals can achieve comparable recommendation quality. On Office with SASRec, LoopRec achieves higher mean NDCG@20 than either the position-based or frequency-based heuristic over five seeds. The experimental setup and full results are provided in Appendix A.6.

5 Related Work
Sequential Recommendation. Sequential recommendation mod-
els an ordered interaction history to rank the next item. Early
factorized and neural approaches capture local transition struc-
ture via Markov chains, recurrent networks, or convolutional en-
coders [8, 14, 17, 22, 28, 34]. Transformer-based recommenders
such as SASRec and BERT4Rec then strengthen long-range depen-
dency modeling with self attention [12, 15, 19, 27, 30, 38]. More
recent fixed-depth backbones refine the encoder design with ex-
plicit inductive biases, for instance through frequency-domain or
filtering mechanisms [3, 26, 39]. These methods focus on how to
build stronger sequence encoders under a fixed computation pattern
: once the architecture is chosen, each history position is processed
by the same depth budget before scoring the next item. LoopRec
addresses an orthogonal question. Keeping the recommendation
objective and backbone family intact, it asks whether a sequential
encoder can allocate recursive computation at the item level, so
that different positions in the same history need not receive the
same depth.
Looped and Adaptive-Depth Transformers. Looped Trans-
formers study the repeated application of shared or partially shared
Transformer blocks. The Universal Transformer combines shared
recurrent transformations with self-attention and supports adap-
tive per-position halting [2], building on adaptive computation
time [7]. Later work shows that looped Transformers can imple-
ment non-trivial algorithmic computation [6, 33]. Recent looped
Transformer and looped language-model studies connect repeated
depth with latent computation and reasoning [23, 41]. In parallel,
adaptive-depth Transformers explore early exiting or routed com-
putation allocation [4, 18, 21, 24, 31, 40]. Mixture-of-Recursions
(MoR) combines shared recursion with token-level adaptive com-
putation for language modeling [1]. Its token-choice router assigns

sections.title:
6 Conclusion
We revisited fixed-depth computation in sequential recommenda-
tion through diagnostic experiments that reveal heterogeneous
depth sensitivity across history items. Motivated by these find-
ings, we proposed LoopRec, which uses weight-shared recursion
with learned item-wise routing to allocate computation adaptively.
Across three Amazon benchmarks and four backbone families,
LoopRec consistently improves ranking performance over fixed-
depth counterparts. Its learned routes allocate greater depth to re-
cent and less frequent items, consistent with the patterns observed
in these diagnostics. LoopRec also reduces the encoder computa-
tion budget in the measured configurations, although latency gains
vary. Future work includes developing sparsity-aware kernels and
learning the maximum recursion budget, which is currently fixed
per configuration before model training begins.
